Indeterminacy is the state or condition of being not determined — meaning not fixed, not settled, not pinned down to a single clear answer, outcome, or meaning.

When something has indeterminacy, it remains genuinely open. It resists being nailed down to one definite, certain value or interpretation. Multiple possibilities exist simultaneously, and there is no obvious, final way to resolve them into just one.

The word comes from the adjective "indeterminate," and adding "-cy" turns that into a noun — so indeterminacy names the quality or condition of being indeterminate, the same way "accuracy" names the quality of being accurate.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine you ask someone, "How tall is a tall person?" They might say "six feet," but someone else might say "five-ten," and another person might say "it depends." There is no single, fixed, universally correct height at which "not tall" becomes "tall." The boundary is blurry and unresolvable. That blurriness — that absence of a definite, fixed answer — is indeterminacy.

Now take a harder example. Imagine a quantum particle — something unimaginably tiny, like an electron. Before a scientist looks at it, the electron does not have a single fixed location. It exists spread across many possible positions at once. It is not that we simply don't know where it is, the way you don't know what's inside a wrapped gift. The electron genuinely, truly has no single location yet. It is spread out in possibility-space. That fundamental openness in nature itself is indeterminacy at its most powerful.

These two examples — one gentle and everyday, one deep and scientific — show you the range of the word. At its weakest, indeterminacy means something is fuzzy and unclear. At its strongest, it means something is fundamentally, irreducibly open — not just unknown, but undecided at its very core.
How Indeterminacy Differs From Similar Words

This word lives in a neighborhood with several close relatives — uncertainty, ambiguity, and vagueness — and mixing them up is easy. Here is how they differ.

Uncertainty is about the limits of your knowledge. You are uncertain when you don't know something that nevertheless has a fixed, real answer. If a coin is already flipped and covered by a hand, you are uncertain which side is up — but one side is up. The fact is settled; you just can't see it. Uncertainty is a problem in your mind, not in the world.

Ambiguity is when a word, sentence, or situation has two or more distinct, clear meanings, and you can't tell which one is intended. "I'm going to the bank" — are you going to a financial bank or a riverbank? Those are two crisp, definite meanings. The ambiguity is about which one the speaker meant. Crucially, there is a correct answer; you just don't have enough context to find it.

Vagueness is when the edges of a concept or word are unclear. "Bald," "tall," "old," "a heap" — these words don't have a sharp boundary. There's no precise number of hairs that separates bald from not-bald. Vagueness is a feature of language and meaning.

Indeterminacy is broader and deeper than all three. It can overlap with them, but at its core it refers to a genuine, principled absence of a single fixed fact of the matter. It isn't merely that you don't know (uncertainty), or that two meanings could apply (ambiguity), or that an edge is fuzzy (vagueness). Indeterminacy says: there simply is no one correct, settled answer — the thing itself is open. This can be true of nature, of meaning, of law, of art, and more.

The word is used across many disciplines, and learning its use in each one deepens your feel for it enormously.

In Physics

This is where the word gets its most famous and dramatic use. In quantum mechanics — the science of the very smallest things — Werner Heisenberg showed that certain pairs of properties of a particle, such as its position and its momentum (how fast it's moving and in what direction), cannot both be precisely known or even precisely defined at the same time. The more precisely you pin down one, the more smeared-out and undefined the other becomes.

This is not a failure of our measuring instruments. It is not a problem that better technology would fix. It is a fundamental feature of physical reality. The particle does not have a precise position and a precise momentum simultaneously. Before you measure it, it exists in a blur of possibilities — a superposition. Measurement forces it to "choose" one definite value, but before that moment, the indeterminacy is real and absolute. This is called quantum indeterminacy, and it shook the foundations of science because it showed that nature, at its deepest level, is not fully determined in advance.

In Philosophy

Philosophers use indeterminacy in several important ways.

In debates about free will and the nature of reality, the question is whether the future is determined — fixed in advance by prior causes, like a chain of dominoes — or genuinely indeterminate — open and not yet settled. If the future has indeterminacy, then events have real openness, and free will becomes more plausible. If everything is determined, then indeterminacy is an illusion.

Philosophers also speak of metaphysical indeterminacy — the idea that some facts about the world are genuinely not settled. For instance, when exactly does a person cease to be alive? Is there a precise, fixed moment that is the true boundary? Or is the world itself vague on this point? If the latter, that is metaphysical indeterminacy — the world, not just our language or knowledge, is indeterminate.

In Language and Meaning

Philosophers of language speak of semantic indeterminacy — the idea that words and sentences sometimes do not have a single, fixed, correct meaning, even in principle.

The philosopher W.V.O. Quine argued for something called the indeterminacy of translation — the idea that when you translate from one language to another, there can be multiple, equally valid translations that are genuinely different, with no deeper fact about the world that settles which one is truly correct. This is a radical and controversial idea, but it uses "indeterminacy" in a powerful way: not just "it's hard to choose the best translation," but "there is no single fact of the matter about the correct translation."

More simply, semantic indeterminacy shows up whenever you try to define a word precisely and find that the word resists a clean, crisp boundary — not because you haven't thought hard enough, but because the concept itself does not carve reality at clean joints.

In Law

Legal scholars speak of legal indeterminacy — the idea that laws and legal texts do not always produce a single, determinate correct answer when applied to cases. A law might be written in broad language that could be interpreted in multiple, genuinely valid ways. No amount of careful reading automatically produces one correct answer; judges exercise judgment and discretion to fill in the gaps.

This is important because it challenges the idea that law is a precise machine that simply computes the right verdict. Legal indeterminacy suggests that law has built-in openness — it is not fully determined, and real human judgment is always involved in applying it.

In Art and Music

In 20th-century avant-garde music and art, indeterminacy became an intentional artistic choice. Composers like John Cage created indeterminate music — compositions in which certain elements were deliberately left open: the performer might choose the order of sections, or the timing, or some notes. No two performances would be the same because the work itself was not fully fixed in advance. The artwork was not a determined object; it was a set of open possibilities that became real in the act of performance. This celebrated indeterminacy as a creative value, not a problem to be solved.

Across all these uses, the word "indeterminacy" always points to the same essential idea: the absence of a single, fixed, settled answer or state.

Whether it is a quantum particle with no definite position, a legal text with no clearly correct interpretation, a word with no sharp boundary, or a musical piece with no fixed final form — in every case, something that could be fixed, resolved, or settled into one definite answer simply is not. It remains open, floating, plural in its possibilities.

The opposite of indeterminacy is determinacy — the state of being fixed, decided, precise, and singular. A mathematical equation like 2 + 2 = 4 has full determinacy: there is one correct answer, always, with no openness whatsoever. Indeterminacy is everything on the other end of that spectrum — from mild fuzziness all the way to fundamental, irreducible openness.

If you had to compress the entire word into one sentence: Indeterminacy is the condition of being genuinely open, unfixed, and unresolvable to a single clear answer — whether in the behavior of nature, the meaning of language, the outcome of events, or the interpretation of rules.
